title: Magnify the substrate: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Magnify the substrate from a 300 mm wafer (0.07 m2) to a 2.2x2.5 m display-glass mother panel (~80x the area) and build oxide-TFT 2T gain-cell arrays on idle LCD/LTPO backplane lines, dicing panels into memory tiles bonded to silicon periphery.
why: Capital intensity and throughput: depreciated LCD fabs cost cents per cm2 versus ~$10+/cm2 for DRAM wafers; area cost per bit could fall 10x even at relaxed F, turning global display overcapacity into memory capacity.

title: Minify the fab: half-inch wafer micro-fabs for distributed DRAM
idea: Minify the wafer to 12.5 mm and the tool to a desk-sized, cleanroom-free unit (Minimal-Fab style sealed shuttle), then run a simple gain-cell DRAM flow in hundreds of $5M micro-fabs placed next to data centers instead of one $15B megafab.
why: Capital intensity and time-to-capacity: capacity can be added in $5M increments in months, not $15B in 4 years; US manufacturability through many small sites.

title: Relax F to 38 nm, magnify tiers to 300
idea: Minify lithography demand by freezing lateral pitch at a DUV-immersion 38 nm and magnify vertical tiers to 300 using NAND-style alternating deposition, one hole etch per 50 tiers, and a vertical-channel gain cell, so deposition and etch replace EUV.
why: Litho-bound scaling and EUV dependence: zero EUV layers; density grows with deposition tools costing ~1/4 of an EUV scanner per wafer-pass, targeting >2x bits per wafer at lower capex per bit.

title: One-mask cell array via self-aligned everything
idea: Minify array masks to one: a single DUV mandrel feeds self-aligned quadruple patterning in two orthogonal directions, and every later array layer (contacts, landing pads, capacitor holes) is defined by selective deposition and etch keyed to the prior topography, never by an overlay exposure.
why: Masks and EUV count: array EUV layers fall from 5-7 to 0 and array mask count drops roughly 80%, removing overlay error budgets and cutting litho share of wafer cost by about half.

title: Full-wafer single-shot nanoimprint of each array layer
idea: Magnify the imprint field from one 26x33 mm die to the whole 300 mm wafer: a flexible quartz-on-glass master imprints every array layer in a single press using thermal-expansion-matched chucks and in-situ moire alignment.
why: Lithography throughput and tool cost: one press per wafer replaces ~100 scanner shots; tool cost ~$15-30M versus ~$200M EUV, targeting >5x lower litho cost per wafer layer.

title: Ten-million-beam maskless e-beam wafer writer
idea: Magnify the beam count of multibeam mask writers by 100x to 10 million individually blanked beams on a MEMS aperture plate, with array rasters stored as one repeated tile, so DRAM layers are written maskless at ~50 wafers/hour.
why: EUV single-supplier risk and mask cost: removes EUV and multi-million-dollar mask sets; a US-buildable electron-optics tool chain.

title: Talbot self-imaging lithography for perfectly periodic arrays
idea: Exploit that the DRAM array is a perfect lattice: minify the optics to zero by using lensless Talbot/interference self-imaging of a periodic grating, magnifying the coherent print area to the full wafer for all array layers.
why: Litho capital: lens-free optics cost <5% of a scanner; 193 nm interference can print ~40 nm pitch lattices with infinite depth of focus, and periphery stays on cheap DUV.

title: Periphery on legacy 200 mm US fabs, bonded to array
idea: Minify what needs a leading-edge fab to only the dense cell array; make the 49% periphery (sense amps, decoders, I/O) on underused 200/300 mm mature-node US fabs, then wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond the two.
why: Periphery die area and capital: frees ~half of expensive DRAM wafer area for bits (~1.8x density per DRAM wafer) and reuses depreciated US fabs for the logic half.

title: Frozen-node DRAM: depreciate tools over fifteen years
idea: Minify node changes to zero: design a DRAM generation that never shrinks and is upgraded only by stacking more dies per package, so tools run 15 years instead of a 5-year depreciation schedule.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost; tripling tool life cuts wafer cost roughly 30-35%, while a node only buys 10-20%.

title: Container fab: kill the ballroom cleanroom
idea: Minify the cleanroom from a 100,000 m2 ballroom to sealed mini-environments around each tool inside standard shipping containers, linked by sealed-pod conveyors, so the building is an ordinary warehouse.
why: Fab construction capital: cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab cost and years of build; target 3-4x faster capacity add.

title: Inductive coupling replaces TSVs in stacked DRAM
idea: Minify die-to-die vias to zero: thin each die to 10 um and pass data through on-chip inductor coils stacked over each other, with power delivered through a single edge-plated rail, removing TSV etch, liner, fill and reveal.
why: HBM TSV tax: removes the TSV process module and its 20-30% yield loss, recovering area spent on TSV keep-out zones.

title: DRAM in the metal layers of any logic wafer
idea: Magnify where memory can be made: build a low-temperature (<400 C) gain-cell DRAM inside the BEOL interconnect stack of foundry logic wafers as two extra metal levels, so no dedicated DRAM fab is needed.
why: Capital intensity: piggybacks on existing logic fab capacity worldwide, including US foundries; incremental cost is a few masks rather than a new $15B fab.

title: Self-ordering anodic alumina templates for capacitor holes
idea: Minify capacitor-hole lithography to zero: anodize a deposited aluminum film so it self-organizes into a hexagonal nanopore lattice (aspect ratio >100), then line pores with electrode and high-k by ALD.
why: Capacitor charge wall and EUV layers: electrochemistry in a beaker replaces the hardest EUV and high-AR etch step; pores naturally reach AR ~115+.

title: High-chi block copolymer multiplies DUV hole density fourfold
idea: Magnify density without new optics: coarse DUV guide posts direct a high-chi block copolymer to self-assemble 4 cylinders per guide at ~12 nm, used for landing pads and storage-node contacts.
why: Lithography: removes 1-2 EUV layers per die; DSA tooling is a track, not a scanner.

title: Dirty fab: class-1000 cleanroom plus massive remapping
idea: Minify cleanliness requirements 1000x and magnify redundancy: accept up to 30% bad bits per subarray and let a controller with an on-die defect map route around them like a Teramac crossbar.
why: Fab capital and yield: cleanroom spend and particle control capex fall sharply; dies that would be scrapped become sellable at derated capacity.

title: Reusable parent wafer: porous-silicon layer transfer
idea: Minify Czochralski crystal use: grow a thin epitaxial silicon device layer on a porous-silicon release layer, transfer it to a cheap carrier, and reuse the parent wafer 50+ times.
why: Scarce resources: cuts high-purity quartz crucible and polysilicon demand (Spruce Pine chokepoint) per wafer by >90%.

title: Rotary spatial ALD at atmospheric pressure
idea: Magnify deposition throughput 10x by spinning wafers under fixed precursor zones separated by gas curtains (spatial ALD) at atmospheric pressure for capacitor high-k and liners, instead of slow pulsed vacuum ALD.
why: Throughput and tool cost: ALD is a bottleneck in capacitor and 3D flows; 10x fewer chambers per wafer start.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM: no dicing, no packaging
idea: Magnify the die to the whole wafer: one 300 mm wafer becomes one memory module with wafer-level redundancy and a bonded edge connector, skipping dicing, die sort, packaging and module assembly.
why: Back-end capital and test: removes packaging steps and per-die test overhead; one terabyte-class memory per wafer for rack-scale systems.

title: Combinatorial coupon line for 100x faster process learning
idea: Minify experiments to 25 mm coupons with gradient deposition and run 1000 process splits per week on a high-throughput pilot line, so new-cell development needs a $50M line, not a full fab.
why: Development time and capital: compresses 3-5 year node learning toward 1 year and lowers entry cost for US newcomers.

title: Programmable photomask for periphery layers
idea: Minify mask-set cost to zero for non-critical layers by exposing through a 193 nm-compatible spatial light modulator (micromirror array) that reprograms its pattern per layer and per product.
why: Masks: a DRAM mask set costs millions of dollars; periphery variants and test chips become free to iterate.

title: Multi-level DRAM: two bits per capacitor relax lithography
idea: Magnify bits per cell to 2 using four charge levels and a reference-ladder sense amp with refresh-time calibration, buying a node of density without a shrink.
why: Litho-bound scaling: about 2x density at the same F, worth more than a 10-20% node; no new EUV layers.

title: Helium-free chucks using liquid-metal backside contact
idea: Minify helium use to zero: replace helium backside cooling in etch and deposition chucks with a thin gallium-alloy film or compliant metal pads that conduct heat to the wafer.
why: Scarce resource: helium supply (Qatar ~30%, offline) currently gates fab output; removes a chokepoint for every wafer step.

title: Aircraft-style leasing of fab tools across memory makers
idea: Magnify tool ownership to third-party lessors who buy EUV, etch and deposition tools and lease them, redeploying tools between memory makers as cycles shift, like aircraft leasing.
why: Capital intensity: moves $10B+ off the maker's balance sheet, raises tool utilization, and lowers the hurdle for a new US entrant.

title: Kilometer-scale web: printed gain-cell memory sheets
idea: Magnify the substrate to a 1 m-wide polyimide web moving at 10 m/min, printing oxide 2T gain cells at 20 um2 per bit (~6 GB per m2), used as a capacity tier behind an SRAM/DRAM cache.
why: Capital intensity: a roll-to-roll line costs ~$20-50M; at ~$20/m2 this targets a few dollars per GB with zero EUV.

title: Self-aligned imprint: all layer masks in one stamp
idea: Minify alignment steps to zero by encoding all layer geometries as stepped heights in one 3D roll-to-roll imprint stamp; successive etch-backs reveal each level, so layers are perfectly registered even on a stretching web.
why: Masks and overlay: 6-8 aligned lithography steps collapse into one imprint, which makes fine pitch possible on flexible substrates.

title: Printing-press nanoimprint drum for continuous wafer streams
idea: Magnify lithography throughput 20x by passing wafers on a conveyor under a rotating nanoimprint drum carrying the array pattern, printing one layer per second like a newspaper press.
why: Litho tool cost and throughput: ~3600 wafer-layers per hour versus ~150 for EUV, from a drum tool costing a fraction of a scanner.

title: Electrohydrodynamic jet printing of maskless periphery wiring
idea: Minify the mask count of interconnect layers to zero: multi-nozzle EHD jets print sub-100 nm silver/copper lines for periphery routing straight from CAD, so every wafer can carry custom wiring or repair routes.
why: Masks and BEOL capital: removes metal masks and the litho-etch loop for those levels; gives instant design iteration.

title: Gravure-printed redox molecules as storage capacitors
idea: Magnify charge per area by printing a monolayer of porphyrin or ferrocene redox molecules; each molecule stores discrete electrons faradaically, so a planar printed cell stores what a 70:1 pillar does.
why: Capacitor charge wall: about 10x charge density per footprint, which removes high-AR capacitor etch from the process.

title: Printed relaxor polymer dielectric hitting k near 60
idea: Magnify dielectric constant by slot-die coating P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) relaxor terpolymer (k~50-60) biased in its non-switching paraelectric regime as a planar storage capacitor dielectric.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Fact 1 needs k~70 to escape the pillar; a printed planar capacitor with k~60 approaches it at ~1/10 the process cost.

title: Laminated foil stack: 100 printed sheets per block
idea: Magnify tiers through lamination instead of deposition: print memory on 10 um foils, laminate 100 foils into a 1 mm block, and connect them through laser-drilled, printed-fill vertical edge vias.
why: 3D DRAM tier problem: 100 tiers with no tier-by-tier deposition yield compounding, because each foil is tested before lamination.

title: Vertical printed transistors: channel length set by film thickness
idea: Minify channel length to ~100 nm without fine lithography by building vertical printed transistors in which source and drain are stacked layers and the channel is the coated film thickness.
why: Speed and litho: printed transistors reach switching speeds near what a 10-100 ns DRAM access needs, using only micron-scale patterning.

title: One microcontact stamp sets surface energy for every ink
idea: Minify patterning to a single microcontact-printed self-assembled monolayer pattern; every following functional ink is blade-coated and de-wets into the matching wells by surface energy, self-aligned across layers.
why: Process steps and alignment: one stamp replaces several print-align steps, and cuts material waste by >90%.

title: Liquid-silane ink laser-annealed into roll-to-roll polysilicon
idea: Magnify printed transistor mobility about 10x by coating cyclopentasilane ink and laser-crystallizing it into polysilicon on the web, giving ~100 cm2/Vs access and sense transistors.
why: Speed of printed memory: makes the printed tier fast enough for near-DRAM latency without vacuum front-end tools.

title: Transistor-free crosspoint: printed threshold selector plus capacitor
idea: Minify the cell to 4F2 by printing crossed wordlines and bitlines, with a volatile Ag-filament threshold switch in series with a planar capacitor at each crossing as the access device.
why: Density and process steps: no transistor layers in the array, so 2-3 printed layers make a full array.

title: Printed electric double-layer storage capacitors
idea: Magnify areal capacitance about 1000x by printing an ionic-gel film whose electric double layer (~10 uF/cm2) stores the bit's charge in a tiny planar footprint.
why: Capacitor charge wall: fF-scale charge in sub-um2 area with no pillar; the open risk is ion response time at ns speeds.

title: Retrofit idle web presses into printed-memory lines
idea: Minify fab capex to ~$20M per line by converting idle US newspaper and packaging web presses into memory lines, adding laminar-flow tunnels around the web path and inline photonic/laser stations.
why: US manufacturability and capital: reuses US industrial plants and skilled press workforce; capacity added in months.

title: Inline print-test-repair loop with capacitive probe rollers
idea: Magnify test throughput by running the web past non-contact capacitive probe rollers that map bad blocks in real time; a downstream laser cuts and a printer reroutes around them before lamination.
why: Yield and test capital: testing at web speed removes probe-card floors and turns defects into reroutes, not scrap.

title: Print memory directly on package substrate panels
idea: Magnify memory placement onto 510x515 mm organic package panels: inkjet-print oxide gain-cell arrays beside the processor footprint during panel-level packaging, so memory and package are made in one line.
why: Data movement and capital: millimeters from the compute die, no separate memory wafer, and it uses existing panel-packaging lines.

title: Micro-transfer printing 100 um DRAM chiplets onto panels
idea: Minify the die to 100 um chiplets made at a mature node, then magnify deployment by elastomer-stamp transfer printing 100,000 chiplets per stroke onto large panels with printed interconnect.
why: Yield and capital: tiny dies yield near 100%, mature nodes avoid EUV, and panel-scale assembly replaces per-die packaging.

title: Single ink whose function is set by laser dose
idea: Minify materials from six inks to one: print one In-Zn oxide precursor everywhere, then a laser dose map sets each region as conductor, semiconductor or insulator by controlling oxygen-vacancy density.
why: Process steps and tool count: one print station plus one digital laser replaces multiple deposition-litho-etch loops.

title: Micro-banks: sixteen cells per printed bitline
idea: Minify the bitline to 16 cells and magnify the bank count to millions, each tiny sub-array with its own printed sense amplifier, so printed-wire RC drops about 64x.
why: Latency of printed memory: brings slow printed arrays toward ~100 ns access, trading area for speed on cheap area.

title: Electrochemically exfoliated MoS2 ink for low-leakage access devices
idea: Magnify off-state resistance by printing electrochemically exfoliated MoS2 nanosheet inks (1.8 eV gap) as the access transistor channel, so leakage is low enough for long retention.
why: Refresh: wide-bandgap printed channels cut leakage far below the 13 fA tail, stretching refresh intervals on cheap printed arrays.

title: Flash-lamp photonic curing makes ceramic dielectrics on plastic
idea: Minify thermal budget with millisecond xenon flash pulses that heat only the printed film to ~1000 C, sintering dense oxide dielectrics and conductors on a polymer web without damaging it.
why: Process energy and capital: replaces furnaces and vacuum annealing, enabling quality storage dielectrics at web speed.

title: Page-wide 100,000-nozzle printhead deposits only where needed
idea: Magnify nozzle count to a page-wide MEMS printhead array firing sub-femtoliter drops across the full web, depositing dielectric and electrode only where cells exist instead of blanket coating plus etch.
why: Material and step count: about 95% less material waste, and no litho-etch loop for coarse layers.

title: Rolling film masks printed for pennies
idea: Minify mask cost from ~$300k to under $100 by roll-printing flexible photomasks and using rolling near-field contact lithography to pattern non-critical DRAM layers.
why: Masks: disposable printed masks for periphery and BEOL layers cut mask-set spend and lead time.

title: Printed memory prize: 1 GB per square meter
idea: Minify entry capital with a US milestone prize (target: 1 GB per m2 at under $5/m2 and 100 ns latency) tied to a shared open roll-to-roll pilot line where teams rent web time by the meter.
why: US manufacturability and capital: dozens of teams can try printed DRAM approaches without each building a line.
